_doc: One NHC advisory for one storm. Times are UTC ('YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MMZ'). past_track rows = [time, lat, lon, vmax_kt, mslp_mb, status]. forecast: tau 0 = advisory time; other taus count from the synoptic hour (advisory time rounded down to 00/06/12/18Z), like NHC. status: TD/TS/HU/MH (tropical), PT (post-tropical), LO (remnant low), DS (dissipated; no position). radii (nmi by quadrant) keyed '34','50','64', optional '12ft' seas (tau 0 only). coastal_ww segments run breakpoint-to-breakpoint using names in data/tc_breakpoints.json; types HU.W, HU.A, TR.W, TR.A. inland_ww are county lists ('Name ST') drawn as shaded counties (optional; set cone.show_inland false for a pure NHC look). cone.radii_nmi is ILLUSTRATIVE and configurable, not an official NHC table. text = hand-written narrative pieces for the TCP/TCM.
name: Delphine
changes: The Hurricane Warning has been extended westward to the Okaloosa/Walton County Line.
A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued from the Alabama/Florida Border to the Okaloosa/Walton County Line.

cone._doc: Radii in nautical miles by forecast hour. ILLUSTRATIVE values in the spirit of NHC's 2-in-3 track-error circles; edit freely.

headlines: DELPHINE ACCELERATING RAPIDLY TOWARD THE FLORIDA PANHANDLE...EXPECTED TO MAKE LANDFALL AS A MAJOR HURRICANE THIS EVENING
CATASTROPHIC STORM SURGE WILL RISE VERY QUICKLY FROM MEXICO BEACH TO THE BIG BEND TONIGHT
DESTRUCTIVE HURRICANE-FORCE WINDS WILL SPREAD NORTH ALONG THE GEORGIA-ALABAMA LINE OVERNIGHT...WITH THE ATLANTA METRO AREA IN THE STRONGEST PART OF THE STORM
text.track: Delphine is expected to accelerate further tonight as it is captured by a strong mid-level trough over the lower Mississippi Valley, with forward speeds of 40 to 50 mph. On the forecast track, the center of Delphine will reach the Florida Panhandle coast near Mexico Beach between 8 and 9 PM EDT, then race northward near the Georgia-Alabama border overnight, passing near Columbus and LaGrange and about 40 miles west of downtown Atlanta around 2 AM EDT Saturday. Delphine is expected to turn north and slow down as it merges with the trough over the Ohio Valley Saturday and Sunday.
text.intensity_extra: Little change in strength is expected before landfall. Because of Delphine's extremely fast forward speed, only gradual weakening is expected as it moves across Georgia tonight, and it is forecast to still be a hurricane when it reaches the Atlanta area. Delphine is forecast to become a powerful post-tropical cyclone over the southern Appalachians Saturday morning as it merges with the trough. Its wind field will expand, and damaging winds will extend far from the center through the weekend.
text.watch_extra: Hurricane and Tropical Storm Warnings are in effect well inland from local National Weather Service offices, including the Atlanta, Columbus, and Macon metropolitan areas and portions of east Alabama. Because of Delphine's speed, conditions will deteriorate very rapidly tonight. Preparations should be rushed to completion early this evening. For storm information specific to your area, please monitor products issued by your local National Weather Service forecast office.
hazards: The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded by rising waters moving inland from the shoreline. Because of Delphine's fast motion, the water will rise very rapidly, in some places by several feet in less than an hour. The water could reach the following heights above ground somewhere in the indicated areas if the peak surge occurs at the time of high tide...
- Mexico Beach to Ochlockonee River, FL, including Apalachicola...14-20 ft
- Ochlockonee River to Suwannee River, FL...10-15 ft
- Suwannee River to Anclote River, FL...5-8 ft
- Walton/Bay County Line to Mexico Beach, FL, including Panama City...6-10 ft
- Okaloosa/Walton County Line to Walton/Bay County Line, FL...3-5 ft

Hurricane conditions are expected within the Hurricane Warning area along the coast this evening. Destructive hurricane-force winds will spread north overnight along and east of the Georgia-Alabama border, including Columbus, LaGrange, and the entire Atlanta metropolitan area, which will be in the dangerous right-front quadrant of the storm. Gusts of 100 to 120 mph are possible from Columbus to Atlanta and Gainesville. After two days of heavy rain, soils are saturated across north Georgia, so widespread tree falls, structural damage, and power outages lasting days to weeks are expected. Many of these winds will occur in the middle of the night. Residents should be in their safe place, away from trees and windows, before winds increase this evening.

A predecessor rain event has already produced 6 to 12 inches of rain across north Georgia since Wednesday, including about 10 inches at Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport. Delphine will produce an additional 3 to 6 inches of rain, with isolated totals near 8 inches, across Georgia, the western Carolinas, and the southern Appalachians through Saturday. On top of saturated ground and running-high streams, this will cause considerable to catastrophic flash and urban flooding and significant to major river flooding. Landslides are possible in the southern Appalachians.

Several tornadoes are possible tonight and early Saturday across the eastern Florida Panhandle, north Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina. These tornadoes will be moving very quickly and will be wrapped in rain, in many cases overnight.
Swells generated by Delphine are affecting much of the Gulf Coast and the west coast of Florida. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.

_scenario: Alternate 'fast + west' Delphine: Mexico Beach landfall, center up the GA-AL line ~40 mi west of Atlanta, metro in the right-front quadrant.
